title: Corrections to the IPR in the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice
summary: We show that finite-size effects in the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice are highly anomalous. On random regular graphs of $N$ sites the inverse participation ratio (IPR) approaches its thermodynamic-limit value as $I_2(N)-I_2^\infty\sim N^{-\kappa(W)}$, with a disorder-dependent exponent $0<\kappa<1$ throughout the localized phase, and the same exponent governs the correction due to a finite imaginary regulator, $I_2(\eta)-I_2^\infty\sim\eta^{\kappa(W)}$. We derive $\kappa = 2\beta-1$, with $\beta$ the power-law tail exponent of the local density of states distribution, in a solvable model sharing the criticality of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice. We then show that the same mechanism operates in the Anderson model itself, and find quantitative agreement with the numerics. A self-consistent one-loop treatment of the loops of finite graphs independently reproduces the finite-size corrections. Physically, a spectral identity and an exact sum rule tie both corrections to rare Mott-like resonances hybridizing distant localized eigenstates: a finite graph lacks the resonant pairs whose centers would lie farther apart than its size allows. Our results identify the scaling variable needed to extrapolate IPR data to the thermodynamic limit.

title: Anomalous corrections to the inverse participation ratio in the localized phase on the Bethe lattice: insights from a solvable "toy" non-linear $\sigma$-model
summary: In the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice, the inverse participation ratio (IPR) approaches its asymptotic value as the imaginary regulator $\eta \to 0$ with an anomalous power law, $I_2(\eta) - I_2^\infty \propto \eta^{2\beta-1}$, where $\beta \in (1/2,1)$ is the tail exponent of the local density of states distribution. We derive it analytically in a "toy" non-linear $\sigma$-model on the hyperbolic superplane, which shares the exotic criticality of the Bethe-lattice Anderson transition. Matching the bulk solution of its cavity equation to a boundary layer set by the symmetry-breaking field $H$ gives a correction $\propto H^{2\beta-1}$, controlled by the subdominant root $1-\beta$ of the linearized equation; at criticality it becomes $\propto 1/|\ln H|$. Under a few natural assumptions the same mechanism operates in the Anderson model, where the correction is a zero mode of the $\eta=0$ cavity recursion, as we confirm numerically, also for finite-size corrections. Through a spectral identity and an exact sum rule, the same exponent fixes exactly the decay $\omega^{-\mu}$, with $\mu = 2(1-\beta)$, of the correlation function of two eigenstates at energy distance $\omega$, including its amplitude, as we confirm by exact diagonalization, population dynamics on the infinite lattice, and analytically in the toy model. A counting of Mott resonances between distant localized eigenstates explains this physically; on finite graphs, finite-size corrections reflect a deficit of doubly-peaked eigenstates. Finally, we derive the finite-size scaling of the IPR in the variable $(2\beta-1)\ln N$, which describes both finite-$\eta$ and finite-$N$ data. It yields a Kosterlitz-type renormalization-group flow of the running fractal dimension: finite fractal dimensions of localized states at accessible sizes are a logarithmic finite-size effect.

title: Statistical mechanics of linear classification on hierarchical tree data
summary: Deep networks owe much of their success to their ability to exploit the structure in data, from the grammar of language to the multi-scale organization of images. Yet, many statistical mechanics approaches to structured data rely on Gaussian equivalence, whose assumptions can fail when a few latent variables influence all input coordinates. In this work, we take a step beyond this setting with a simple setup, in which a linear classifier is trained to infer the root of the classical broadcast process on a tree from its $N$ leaves. Despite this simplicity, the data already display non-Gaussian statistics along the direction carrying the label, as well as strong finite-size effects. By retaining the exact law along this direction and approximating the transverse fluctuations as Gaussian, we obtain a finite-depth replica theory that accurately describes the measured learning curves. At large depth and sufficiently weak regularization, we uncover a double descent whose two stages are separated in scale. In a range of broadcast noise below the reconstruction threshold, the first descent occurs at a number of samples scaling as $N^\omega$, with $0<\omega<1$ set by the data statistics, whereas the overfitting peak occurs at order $N$ samples. Beyond linear classifiers, this setup could serve as a controlled starting point to study deeper architectures and generative models on hierarchical data.

title: AmorphGen: A Python package for amorphous structure generation with machine-learning and classical interatomic potentials
summary: AmorphGen is an open-source Python package for generating and analyzing amorphous structures from a composition or a crystal. Chemically informed rules estimate initial densities and assign separation and coordination constraints. Three routes are available: random placement followed by relaxation, melt-quench from a crystal, and a hybrid route that anneals and quenches random structures. ASE provides access to classical and machine-learning potentials, with GPU batching for selected backends. Analysis tools compute coordination numbers, bond angles, rings, and X-ray or neutron structure factors for comparison with measurements. An optional interface to the FEFF code computes extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra. For amorphous Ga2O3, TiO2 and InGaZnO4, the cation coordination numbers are close to reference models and measurements, and the X-ray structure factors reproduce the main measured peaks. The EXAFS spectra for Ga2O3 and InGaZnO4 also capture the dominant first-shell features observed experimentally. The hybrid route reduces bonding defects in SiO2 and As and builds the first sharp diffraction peak of SiO2. By simplifying ensemble generation and standardizing structural assessment, AmorphGen makes it practical to compare amorphous models across compositions, potentials, and preparation routes, and to screen new amorphous compositions.

title: Correlated chemical and displacive disorder in a lithium-rich disordered rocksalt revealed by electron diffuse scattering
summary: Lithium transport in disordered rocksalt cathodes depends on local cation arrangements and atomic distortions that are hidden from average-structure analysis. Resolving both contributions experimentally remains challenging, particularly in powders where directional information is lost. Here, we use electron diffuse scattering and three-dimensional difference pair distribution function analysis (3D-{\Delta}PDF) to resolve occupational and displacive correlations in the model lithium-rich rocksalt Li{_2.5}TiO{_3}F{_0.5}. We identify an unusual combination of like-cation first-neighbour and unlike-cation second-neighbour preferences with correlated anion displacements towards Ti and accompanying cation displacements. A minimal pair-interaction model incorporating these displacements reproduces the principal diffuse-scattering and 3D-{\Delta}PDF features and improves agreement with powder-PDF measurements. The experimentally constrained cation configurations exhibit an above-random population of 0-TM lithium-migration environments. These results establish electron 3D-{\Delta}PDF as a route to constrain atomistic models incorporating chemical order and local relaxation, providing a foundation for assessing their combined influence on lithium migration in disordered rocksalt materials.

title: Multiorbital driving of quantum geometric nonlinear transport in oxide interfaces
summary: Quantum geometry plays a relevant role in determining the intrinsic non-linear transport properties of low-dimensional electron systems. Here, we theoretically investigate the quantum geometric contribution to the non-linear conductivity in $\text{SrTiO}_3$-based two-dimensional electron gases, comparing the prototypical (001) and (111) crystallographic interface orientations. Using a multi-orbital tight-binding approach, we uncover the crucial role of the multiband electronic structure in determining the quantum-geometric contribution to nonlinear transport. In particular, we show how the hybridization of $t_{2g}$ orbitals near avoided band crossings shapes the momentum-space distribution of the band-normalized quantum metric and the resulting nonlinear conductivity. Furthermore, we reveal a strong dependence on crystal orientation: while the (001) interface exhibits sharp peak-and-dip features confined around Lifshitz transitions, the trigonal symmetry of the (111) interface promotes strong orbital mixing. Our results highlight how the interplay between orbital hybridization and crystallographic orientation gives rise to distinct quantum-geometric nonlinear transport responses in oxide interfaces.

title: Wireless readout and control of cavity magnon-polaritons via photonic modes delocalised across a gap
summary: In cavity magnonics, photon-magnon hybridisation is typically detected by measuring the cavity response (i.e. measuring cavity resonance shifts through its reflection or transmission spectra). While a large body of work in the field has focused on three-dimensional cavities, a variety of two-dimensional resonators have also been explored as hosts for photonic modes due to their compatibility with on-chip integration. Nevertheless, the readout approach remains largely unchanged. Here, we demonstrate remote excitation and readout of cavity magnon-polaritons using two spatially separated, wirelessly coupled ring resonators. Through inductive coupling, energy is transferred between the resonators, enabling the magnonic system to be excited by one resonator while its hybrid-mode spectrum is detected through measurements of the other. We demonstrate wireless readout of cavity magnon-polaritons at separations ranging from millimetres to centimetres, identifying their characteristic response in the remotely measured spectrum. This establishes wireless resonator coupling as a route to remote interrogation of hybrid photon-magnon systems.

title: Spherical HgTe nanocrystal: a multi-band effective mass study
summary: The size-quantized energies, eigenstates, and optical selection rules in a spherical HgTe nanocrystal are studied by solving the multi-band effective-mass equations analytically. The six-band Kane model, involving both the $\Gamma_{6}$ and $\Gamma_{8}$ bands within the spherical approximation, is employed in the derivation. The eigenstates can be classified by both the total angular momentum and the parity. As the nanocrystal radius varies, crossings occur not only between electron and hole energy levels but also among the hole levels themselves. The lowest two electron states (in each spin subspace) are surface states, one with even parity and the other with odd parity. The optical selection rules consist of two parts, namely, the parity selection and the angular momentum selection.

title: Quantum Hall Effect in a 3D Cross-Dimensional Quantum Anomalous Hall System
summary: We systematically investigate cross-dimensional transport and the resulting quantum Hall effect in 3D quantum anomalous Hall effect systems, which are constructed by coupling two Weyl-semimetal Hamiltonians. Our study unveils that the system hosts highly anisotropic surface states and chiral modes, leading to rich quantum Hall responses. Crucially, we clarify how magnetic fields applied along three high-symmetry directions dictate the evolution of the Chern numbers, chiral modes, and Hall responses. We discover that chiral modes along different directions can originate from distinct mechanisms, giving rise to various magnetic modulation characteristics. Furthermore, we unveil the breakdown of the conventional Chern-number-based bulk-boundary correspondence under magnetic fields, where the Chern numbers alone fail to fully characterize the evolution of the chiral states. This anomalous behavior is attributed to the unique momentum-space distributions of surface bands. These insights are further validated numerically through multi-terminal Hall transport simulations. Our findings expand the understanding of magnetic-field-driven mechanisms in 3D topological systems and provide deeper insights into the interplay between quantized Hall effects and Chern numbers in 3D systems.

title: Local Pressure Induced Quantum Dot to Ring Transition and Aharonov Bohm Effect in Reconfigurable MoTe2 Bilayers
summary: We demonstrate that local pressure provides an effective means of engineering reconfigurable quantum confinement in MoTe2 homobilayers. By applying a smooth, spatially varying pressure profile, we show that the confinement geometry can be continuously tuned from a conventional quantum dot to a quantum ring, with the emergence of annular confinement being a distinctive feature of AB-stacked bilayers. This crossover originates from the pressure-induced spatial modulation in the electronic parameters, which produces an off-center minimum in the effective confinement potential, thereby redistributing the ground-state probability density away from the center and giving rise to an annular confinement geometry. In the quantum-ring regime, a perpendicular magnetic field gives rise to a flux-periodic energy spectrum and persistent currents, providing characteristic signatures of the Aharonov-Bohm effect. By coupling the pressure-induced quantum ring to source and drain leads, we further demonstrate pronounced Aharonov-Bohm conductance oscillations, accompanied by real-space current patterns exhibiting constructive and destructive interference at integer and half-integer magnetic flux quanta, respectively. These findings establish locally pressurized MoTe2 bilayers as a lithography-free platform for reconfigurable quantum confinement and realizing pressure-tunable Aharonov-Bohm interferometry in two dimensional materials.

title: Floquet-Induced Valley Polarization and Topological Phases in Twisted Bilayer Graphene Heterostructures
summary: We theoretically investigate twisted bilayer graphene (tTBG) heterostructures subjected to circularly polarized light. Inversion symmetry is broken through the combined application of an out-of-plane electric field and the incorporation of insulating substrates, enabling precise control of the valley degrees of freedom and associated topological phases. We identify a regime in which the valley degeneracy is lifted: one valley retains a gapless, linear Dirac-like dispersion, whereas the other develops a finite band gap and becomes electronically inactive. The interplay between Floquet driving and inversion-symmetry breaking induces topological phase transitions characterized by Chern numbers C = -2, C = -1, and C = 0, together with the emergence of perfectly valley-polarized domain-wall channels. Furthermore, magnetic asymmetry arising from proximity to adjacent two-dimensional ferromagnetic contacts enables spin-valley filtering. These findings establish the potential of graphene-based heterostructures as highly tunable systems for controlling spin and valley degrees of freedom.

title: Interface invariants of rhombohedral graphene with layer-dependent potentials and couplings
summary: Domain walls in the perpendicular bias of rhombohedral (ABC-stacked) graphene bind valley-resolved interface modes whose signed number is fixed by a bulk-difference invariant. We determine which values of this invariant are reachable when the layer potentials are arbitrary monotone profiles, as produced by screening, and when the interlayer couplings vary from bond to bond. Within the single-particle continuum model, the invariant of an $m$-layer stack equals the difference of occupied angular weights of the zero-momentum levels, which reduces the classification to the ordering of those levels. At equal coupling, nonlinear monotone potentials reproduce exactly the set of invariants of linear potentials, also under the requirement of a common energy gap: screening moves phase boundaries but creates no new invariant values. With bond-dependent coupling, we characterize all occupied configurations. The range of attainable invariants is unchanged, but the gaps inside it are filled, beginning at five layers. Reflection-symmetric stacks realize a large subfamily with a guaranteed common gap, and lower bounds on single-bulk gaps complete the set of invariants with a common global gap for five and six layers. Among the examples is an eight-layer domain wall defined purely by gates, whose number of co-propagating channels per valley switches from 8 to 16 as the gate strength increases. Exact transfer-matrix calculations of the interface spectrum reproduce every predicted signed crossing count. A norm bound gives the minimum spread of interlayer coupling compatible with a prescribed gap.

title: Population of spin orbit-split-electron branches in semimetallic HgTe quantum wells
summary: We present the results of experimental studies on magnetoresistance, the Hall effect, and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations performed in gated heterostructures with HgTe-based gapless semiconductor quantum wells. We show that in quantum wells with widths corresponding to a semimetallic charge carrier spectrum, electrons, in contrast to the idealized model, populate both spin-orbit-split branches of the spectrum. This occurs regardless of whether the Fermi level lies exclusively in the conduction band or within the conduction-valence band overlap region.

title: FlakeForge: automated lithography-ready device layout from optical images of exfoliated van der Waals flakes
summary: Fabricating a device from an exfoliated van der Waals flake requires finding a suitable flake under a microscope and designing its lithography layout by hand. We present FlakeForge, an open-source pipeline from raw optical images of a marker-patterned chip to a lithography-ready, multilayer design file. It scores flakes for device usability, aligns and scales each image from its markers, fits the user's device design to each selected flake's contour and connects every contact to a bond pad by a trace routed around all earlier devices, so no two overlap. Demonstrated on Hall bars and Little-Parks rings, it processed four chips in about half an hour, work that took an expert days. It runs fully unattended or pauses for user review. Adapting it to a new material, marker design or device dimensions requires only configuration, with no training data; a new device type requires only its geometry definition.

title: Kinetic inductance of two-dimensional viscous electron fluid
summary: Modern high-mobility two-dimensional electron systems are pure enough to manifest hydrodynamic regime of electron transport similar to dynamics of classical fluids. With the bulk scattering controlled by momentum-conserving electron-electron collisions, these novel hydrodynamic materials demonstrate systematic violation of conventional metallic behavior due to the Drude model in stationary electric transport. In this letter, we study the linear reactive AC response of 2D electron fluid in a narrow channel geometry and show that the essentially non-local viscous dissipation induces non-trivial size effect in it. In particular, kinetic inductance, which represents collective inertia of the entire electron fluid, is enhanced by non-uniform flow profile and, in contrast to diffusive transport, dominates the electrical impedance already in collisional regime by virtue of viscous skin effect. The onset of reactive behavior falls within the microwave frequency domain in the state-of-the-art 2D hydrodynamic conductors which makes them promising material system for applications in high-frequency electronics at elevated temperatures.

title: Sondheimer oscillations in Weyl semimetal films
summary: In conducting films subject to an out-of-plane magnetic field, electron motion between the surfaces gives rise to conductance oscillations periodic in magnetic field, known as Sondheimer oscillations. While this size effect has been investigated in conventional metals, its dependence on the Berry curvature of topological materials remains less explored. In this work, we extend the semiclassical Boltzmann description of Sondheimer oscillations to type-I Weyl semimetal films. We account for the Berry curvature, the orbital magnetic moment and the effect of the Zeeman coupling on the Fermi wavevector and the electronic group velocity. The Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment generate a beating pattern and chirping in the Sondheimer oscillations. In the thick-film and thin-film regimes, we provide analytical expressions for the longitudinal conductivity, which highlight the interplay between electronic band topology and boundary-scattering in magnetotransport.

title: Geometric Polarization-Virial Theorems for Field-Induced Dipolar Interactions and Force Reversal
summary: Electric fields can turn attraction into repulsion between far-separated atoms, yet the complete angular mechanical structure governing this reversal has remained unknown. Here, we uncover an entropy-like geometric structure: the cubically weighted interaction free energy, r^3 F(r), is nondecreasing under physical dilation. This structure unifies two exact polarization-virial theorems for arbitrary stable quasistatic dipole assemblies and fully retarded dipole pairs under stated conditions. Consequently, the free energy has at most one zero and energetic cancellation precedes mechanical cancellation. A force zero retains strictly positive energy, whereas an energy zero retains an attractive force. The resulting analytical angular fine structure is resolved by a quantum harmonic oscillator pair, yielding the complete arbitrary-angle interaction energy and radial force that recover quantum-perturbative results. The conventional dipolar magic angle splits into strictly ordered energy- and force-zero angles; the latter uniquely bounds the radially repulsive sector and carries a positive energy barrier. Derived scaling laws and finite-sphere calculations provide experimentally testable signatures from microscopic dipoles to macroscopic polarizable bodies.

title: Domain advantage in two-dimensional quantum-device design with multi-modal agentic harness
summary: High-quality two-dimensional quantum devices are commonly fabricated from mechanically exfoliated crystals, whose irregular shapes and placement require a lithographic layout tailored to each specimen. Drawing these layouts remains largely manual. We introduce qlaybench, a benchmark that tests whether language-model agents can turn microscope images and experimental requirements into device layouts that fit the specimen. Agents with conventional tools often construct devices when material outlines are supplied, but struggle to identify those outlines from images. Modelled on the human workflow, qlaybot, a multimodal agentic harness, connects image interpretation to the tools used to align images, draw device features and inspect the resulting layout. We evaluate each layout with checks drawn from practical design experience, asking whether it fits the specimen and connects its intended components. With greater computational effort, an agent using qlaybot passes 81.5% of the benchmark tasks, compared with 24.1% when it uses conventional tools. This domain advantage highlights the importance of connecting scientific interpretation of a specimen to geometric design and provides a route towards reducing manual effort in two-dimensional quantum-device fabrication.

title: A Unified Energy-Density Framework for Moir\'e Interface Energetics and Mechanics
summary: The mechanical response of moir\'e interfaces depends on how atomic registry combines with contact size and boundary geometry. An analytical description must retain this discrete lattice information while connecting microscopic interactions to the energetics of finite contacts. Here, we develop a unified energy-density framework for rigid van der Waals interfaces by expressing registry-dependent pair potentials and atomic densities in reciprocal space. The resulting formulation accommodates different lattice bases and atomic species, linking single-atom and molecular adsorption to infinite bilayers and finite crystalline contacts. Explicit expressions for circular and regular polygonal flakes separate the area contribution from boundary-dependent terms and connect microscopic corrugation coefficients to energy barriers, rotational torques, and interlayer shear stiffnesses. The boundary analysis recovers the quarter-power area scaling of the barrier envelope for circular flakes and distinguishes bounded oscillations from square-root area scaling for polygonal contacts according to edge orientation. A dimensionless criterion characterizes the polygon-to-circle crossover in terms of moir\'e wavelength, flake size, and side number. Direct-summation benchmarks support the finite-domain expressions, while calculations for two-dimensional ice on graphene demonstrate the corresponding boundary-scaling trends in a molecular lattice. Applications to interlayer shear and graphite compression connect the same microscopic interaction description to tangential and normal mechanical responses. The framework establishes an analytical connection between microscopic registry, moir\'e periodicity, and finite-domain geometry, providing a basis for understanding and tailoring the energetics and mechanics of van der Waals contacts.

title: Quantum Geometry Effects in Lattice Dynamics
summary: Quantum geometric effects such as the Berry curvature and the quantum metric are well established in electronic transport, whereas in lattice dynamics the Berry curvature also plays a key role: adiabatically following the lattice, electrons generate a molecular Berry curvature that splits degenerate optical phonons into chiral partners. To determine how the quantum metric affects phonons, we go beyond adiabatic lattice dynamics, identifying Berry curvature and quantum metric contributions to the electronic response of the lattice. Using first-principles calculations in the magnetic topological semimetal EuB$_6$, we find that phonon modes with chiral splitting and those with nonchiral splitting coexist. Unlike the former, which originate from the Berry curvature, the latter arise from the pure quantum metric, while the Berry curvature contribution is forbidden by crystal symmetry.

title: Anatomy of orbital and spin responses in GaAs and Si: Hall, inverse Faraday, and magneto-optical Kerr effects
summary: Magneto-optical signals in nonmagnetic semiconductors entangle spin and orbital contributions, both in angular-momentum generation and magneto-optical detection. We calculate these contributions for electron-doped GaAs and Si using density-functional theory, linear-response theory, and a second-order density-matrix treatment of the inverse Faraday effect. At small electron doping, the intrinsic orbital Hall conductivity exceeds its spin counterpart in magnitude, while the orbital contribution to light-induced magnetization dominates over broad photon-energy ranges. We show that orbital- and spin-resolved optical Hall and polar Kerr coefficients exhibit stronger sensitivity to orbital moments than to equal spin moments. This contrast reflects direct electric-dipole coupling to orbital motion versus spin-orbit-mediated coupling to spin polarization. Consequently, Si maintains a substantial orbital magneto-optical response despite its weak spin-orbit interaction. At probe energies of 1.5 eV in GaAs and 3.0 eV in Si, the magnitude of the Kerr rotation per unit orbital moment is approximately 5 and 13 times larger than that per unit spin moment, respectively. Combining the calculated Hall conductivities and Kerr coefficients with a phenomenological drift-diffusion model yields predominantly orbital edge signals for the assumed diffusion constants and relaxation lengths. These results indicate that optical detection of induced magnetization in doped semiconductors such as GaAs and Si can be dominated by orbital signals, and therefore cannot be interpreted solely in terms of spin polarization.

title: Edge-asymmetric magnetism in semi-Dirac quantum dots
summary: In this study, we investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of quantum dots (QDs) throughout the transition from the Dirac limit to the semi-Dirac limit and beyond. When non-interacting semi-Dirac fermions are confined in triangular QDs, the resulting electronic states near the Fermi level are localized asymmetrically among the three edges of these systems. In the presence of electron interactions, we show that these low-energy states favor the formation of edge-asymmetric magnetism in triangular QDs. In particular, the magnetic moments were localized only along a single edge of the zigzag triangular QDs, corresponding to an edge-asymmetric ferromagnetic ground state. For various system sizes, these zigzag triangular QDs exhibit a one-unit increase in the ground-state total spin ($\Delta S_z = +1$) beyond the semi-Dirac limit, revealing a striking result of this transition. In contrast, the remaining two edges are antiferromagnetically coupled in the armchair triangular QDs, indicating an edge-asymmetric antiferromagnetic (AFM) ground state. We further identified the AFM ground states in hexagonal QDs, indicating that these types of asymmetric configurations are not unique to triangular QDs. Collectively, edge-asymmetric magnetism could create potential opportunities for future spintronics.

title: Scanning nanowire quantum dot with radio-frequency read-out
summary: Scanning single-electron transistors (SETs) are highly sensitive local probes of charge and electric potential, but their integration with robust height control for scanning probe microscopy remains challenging. Furthermore, readout bandwidths are limited to tens of kHz, while characterizing faster charge dynamics is often of interest. Here, we present a scanning SET in the form of a nanowire (NW) quantum dot (QD) integrated at the apex of a non-contact atomic force microscopy (NC-AFM) cantilever. We demonstrate NC-AFM topographic imaging and local electrometry capability by mapping the electrostatic potential generated by a set of nanoscale voltage-biased gate electrodes. Comparison with electrostatic simulations shows agreement with the measured potential profiles. We demonstrate radio-frequency (rf) reflectometry read-out of the sensor, by embedding the QD in an LC-resonator. This platform establishes a route towards high-bandwidth scanning electrometry with simultaneous topographic contrast.

title: All-in-one Spintronic Sensory Neurons for Magnetic Edge Intelligence
summary: Magnetic fields enable non-contact sensing through nonmagnetic materials, offering opportunities for magnetic edge intelligence in autonomous recognition, navigation, and control. However, directly converting magnetic stimuli into neural spikes for local neuromorphic processing remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate an all-in-one spintronic sensory neuron (SSN) based on spin-transfer-torque magnetic tunnel junctions (STT-MTJs) fabricated using a 40-nm magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) process. By exploiting magnetic-field-modulated stochastic switching, the SSN enables probability-based sensing with an electrically tunable sensitive field window, allowing adaptive operation across different magnetic-field ranges without structural modification. This tunability alleviates the fixed sensitivity-range constraint of conventional tunneling magnetoresistance sensing, providing an accessible sensing range of +/-40 mT with an average probability sensitivity of 2.91%/mT. Importantly, the same stochastic switching process directly transduces magnetic stimuli into binary spike trains, integrating magnetic sensing, nonlinear rate encoding, and spike generation within a single nanoscale device. The resulting sigmoidal spike-rate response enables magnetic-field encoding, experimentally validated using the Neural Engineering Framework. Using experimentally characterized device responses, a simulated 10 x 10 SSN array achieves 90.7% accuracy in contactless magnetic-trajectory recognition with optimized encoding, approaching the software baseline. These results establish a scalable, MRAM-compatible approach to unifying programmable magnetic sensing and neural encoding for sensor-native edge intelligence.

title: Two-dimensional Thyristor
summary: Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer a viable platform for next-generation electronics beyond sub-3 nm nodes, yet essential nonlinear circuit elements, such as thyristors, remain unexplored on atomically thin platforms. Here, we report an atomically thin reconfigurable electro-optical thyristor based on a lateral WSe2-MoSe2-WSe2-MoSe2 PNPN heterostructure, directly grown via sequential edge epitaxy. Unlike single-junction 2D diodes, this multijunction architecture exhibits thyristor-like nonlinear switching, including forward blocking, abrupt snapback, bistability, and electrical latching. The device exhibits a forward-blocking voltage of 183 V, corresponding to a critical electric field of 1 MV/cm. Under open-gate conditions, avalanche-assisted carrier multiplication and regenerative feedback are associated with a sharp forward-voltage drop of 175 V, a pronounced current surge, and an ultralow holding voltage. Gate-pulse modulation and temperature-dependent measurements indicate avalanche-assisted thyristor operation and latching behavior. This 2D lateral heterostructure enables a new route to nonlinear and bistable switching, latching, ultralow standby power, and adaptive logic, opening the way for reconfigurable 2D electronics and photonic integrated circuits.

title: Aharonov-Bohm oscillations in transport through interacting quantum dots
summary: We investigate electronic transport through a two-terminal Aharonov-Bohm interferometer with two quantum dots in the presence of finite intra-dot Coulomb interactions. With the help of a diagrammatic technique, we derive, within linear perturbation theory in the tunnelling-coupling strength, analytic expressions for the occupations, current, and interferometric visibility in terms of a coherence measure that involves the sum of four off-diagonal elements of the reduced density matrix. The latter are calculated numerically from a master equation for arbitrary settings of the system parameters. For some symmetric setups, we obtain closed-form expressions for the linear conductance. We systematically analyse the impact of a finite Coulomb interaction on the interferometric visibility, and reveal a rapid suppression of destructive interference upon breaking of system symmetries. Our results are supported by alternative methods, including the TraSPI method.

title: Interaction-driven ordering of multiple pseudospins and anomalous Hall metals in Bernal-stacked graphene
summary: Recent observations of anomalous Hall states in Bernal-stacked tetralayer graphene raise a fundamental question: How do electron-electron interactions organize multiple low-energy pseudospin sectors within each spin-valley flavor? Within the Hartree-Fock approximation, we analyze interaction-driven pseudospin ordering and spin-valley polarization as functions of displacement field and carrier density. We find a rich phase diagram shaped by the interplay between the two pseudospin doublets, including mixed flavor orders at charge neutrality and anomalous Hall metals upon doping. In particular, we identify topological states with $\sigma_{xy} \approx 6e^{2}/h$, consistent with recent experimental observations. Our results highlight the central role of multiple pseudospin doublets in the interaction-driven phases of even-layer Bernal multilayers.

title: Molecular Pawns on a Surface Chessboard: Computational Investigation of Nanographenes with Atomistic Methods
summary: Atomically precise nanographenes combine tunable electronic topology with localized, coherent spin states, making them candidate platforms for molecular quantum technologies. This review examines the multiscale theoretical framework governing these systems: the hierarchy of computational methods for describing magnetic properties, the substrate-molecule interface, on-surface synthetic kinetics, and supramolecular self-assembly. We highlight how density functional theory, automated reaction-path discovery, and spin-aware machine-learned interatomic potentials connect static electronic structure to mesoscale dynamics, and how magnetic exchange, optical excitations, and spin transport can be predicted before synthesis.

title: Dirac-like bands and weak-field transverse transport in ABA trilayer graphene
summary: The low-energy electronic structure of ABA trilayer graphene is composed of light and heavy electron branches, which can be altered by an out-of-plane displacement field. Here, we show that, depending on the values of Slonczewski-Weiss-McClure parameters, a displacement field can inflict a band edge inversion, for which we identify the inversion conditions. This inversion is accompanied by a reversal of Berry curvature and giant topological magnetic moments at the band edges. In a weak perpendicular magnetic field, those topological magnetic moments produce valley splitting, giving rise to distinct anomalous transverse electrical and thermoelectric responses. These features offer a potential route to detecting the band inversion and constraining several of the least established tight-binding parameters, such as the on-site energy shift for the dimer pair of carbons $\Delta^\prime$ and the next neighbour hopping parameters $\gamma_2$ and $\gamma_5$.

title: LeIFF: A localized-electron and ion force field for coupled nuclear and electronic dynamics
summary: Classical and machine-learned interatomic potentials enable large-scale simulations by replacing electronic structure with an effective energy surface for nuclear motion. This excludes electronic dynamics, electronic excitation and energy exchange between electrons and ions. First-principles electron dynamics can describe these processes, but its computational cost restricts system sizes and simulation times. Electron force fields offer an intermediate description by treating electrons as semiclassical dynamical particles interacting with ions. We introduce the localized-electron and ion force field (LeIFF), a compact physical model for both ground state bonding and excited electron dynamics. Valence electrons are represented by spin-labeled spherical charge distributions with dynamical centers and widths. The energy combines analytic electronic kinetic, Coulomb, and dispersion terms with spline-interpolated short-range interactions fitted to a large molecular data set. The resulting energy surface describes a variety of ground state properties across diverse bonding environments and charge states. It also provides a qualitative description of electronic behavior away from equilibrium. It shows improved robustness, accuracy, and transferability relative to earlier electron force-fields. Without any solid-state training, the same model describes dielectric screening and collective electronic response in silicon. LeIFF thus opens a route to large-scale simulations of nonadiabatic processes in molecules and solids, combining chemical bonding and nonequilibrium electronic motion within a common physical framework.

title: Protected Charge Readout Scheme Utilizing Nonlinear Resonators
summary: Charge detection of nanoscale quantum devices commonly relies on dissipative sensors, where signal absorption causes measurement backaction. Recently, nonlinear resonators showed a near-unity readout signal through an induced frequency shift. We show that this frequency shift protects the sensor, as it detunes the resonator from the measurement signal. The resonator excitation reduces while an enhanced readout signal is maintained. Our results, supported by numerical modeling, show that nonlinear resonators can combine strong readout contrast with reduced measurement-induced backaction.

title: Systematically improvable semiclassical clustering for accurate and efficient quantum dynamics in large spin ensembles
summary: Predicting the decoherence of spin qubits in realistic environments is key to identifying the interactions that limit their coherence---a prerequisite for designing better quantum technologies. While accurate methods for spin dynamics are limited to relatively small systems, the dissipative spin environments in real experiments typically involve orders of magnitude more spins. Semiclassical methods can reach these sizes, but their classical treatment of the bath cannot capture the sensor-bath entanglement that generates coherence revivals, especially under the application of refocusing pulses. Here, we resolve this tension. We introduce cluster spin-LSC, a method that clusters the sensor together with a few strongly coupled bath spins, treating them quantum mechanically in an otherwise classical spin bath. We show that our method is applicable to systems containing arbitrary spin species under dynamical decoupling pulse sequences. Our method converges systematically to the exact dynamics with cluster size, providing an internal consistency check when no exact benchmarks exist. We demonstrate that cluster spin-LSC recovers numerically exact coherence and population dynamics for a nitrogen-vacancy center and a molecular qubit, reducing day-long multi-GPU simulations to only minutes on a CPU. We further extend our method to systems with large spin baths that lie beyond the reach of exact methods. Our approach thus offers a scalable and systematically improvable route to accurately simulate the decoherence dynamics of sensors in realistic spin environments.

title: Observation of nonadiabatic quantum tunneling in a driven correlated insulator
summary: Many emerging solid-state platforms for Floquet engineering, nonlinear transport, and high harmonic generation operate near the Keldysh crossover, where optical fields are sufficiently strong and fast to reshape electronic states on sub-cycle timescales. Despite its importance, the microscopic pathways for photocarrier generation in this regime remain poorly understood, as neither perturbative multiphoton absorption nor adiabatic tunneling provides an adequate description. Here, we perform time-resolved optical spectroscopy on the correlated van der Waals insulator NiPS$_3$ while systematically tuning the drive electric field and frequency over a wide range. In the crossover regime, we observe multiphoton-like resonances that are blue-shifted by ponderomotive effects within an otherwise tunneling-dominated absorption channel - a clear spectroscopic signature of adiabaticity breakdown. Hubbard-model simulations based on a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach qualitatively reproduce these features. Together, our results elucidate the microscopic mechanisms of charge excitation in the Keldysh crossover regime and identify a key ingredient for controlling strong-field nonlinear dynamics in correlated materials.

title: Apparent thermal conductivity governed by interface-injected phonon spectra
summary: Thermoreflectance techniques such as time- and frequency-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR and FDTR) are widely used to measure the thermal conductivity of bulk materials, thin films, and interfaces. When phonon mean free paths $\Lambda_\omega$ become comparable to the thermal penetration depth, a Fourier analysis yields an apparent thermal conductivity $\kappa_{\rm app}$ that deviates from the bulk value $\kappa_{\rm bulk}$. Recent studies have highlighted the role of the phonon spectrum injected through the transducer interface, which is generally out of equilibrium owing to frequency-dependent transmission, and have shown that accounting for this nonequilibrium distribution can yield $\kappa_{\rm app}>\kappa_{\rm bulk}$, unlike conventional suppression-function analyses that predict only $\kappa_{\rm app}\leq\kappa_{\rm bulk}$. However, the spectral characteristics governing whether $\kappa_{\rm app}$ is enhanced or reduced remain unclear. Here, we resolve the surface-temperature response of semi-infinite Si mode by mode and show that short-$\Lambda_\omega$-weighted injection raises the surface temperature, whereas long-$\Lambda_\omega$-weighted injection lowers it. This behavior is governed by how deep the injected phonons travel before thermalizing with the lattice, which is set by their mean free paths, and by how effectively the substrate conducts the injected energy away, which is limited by its long-mean-free-path phonons. For an Al (70 nm)/Si structure, Fourier fits of synthetic TDTR phase signals give $\kappa_{\rm app}$ of Si from about 93 to 360 W/(m K) for different interfacial transmission spectra, and $\kappa_{\rm app}$ correlates with the heat-flux-weighted $\Lambda_\omega$ of the transmitted phonons. Thus, $\kappa_{\rm app}$ from thermoreflectance reflects not only the substrate thermal properties but also the phonon spectrum injected across the transducer interface.

title: Spin-controlled thermophase and noise-optimized thermometry in multiorbital quantum dots
summary: Converting temperature differences into electrical signals underlies both thermoelectric energy conversion and thermometry, which is essential for managing heat in cryogenic quantum technologies. Superconducting circuits typically show a weak thermoelectric response, since their quasiparticle spectrum is nearly particle-hole symmetric. In a Josephson junction, a temperature difference can instead be converted into a superconducting phase difference in an open circuit. We investigate this thermophase effect in a setup where the junction consists of a two-orbital quantum dot with Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and Zeeman splitting. A second orbital near the superconducting coherence peaks supports quasiparticle transport over a broad gate range. Zeeman splitting can enhance the thermophase by suppressing pair transport, while spin-orbit hybridization shifts the orbital resonances and can reverse the sign of the response. We assess the junction as a phase-based thermometer using a noise budget that includes readout and current noise together with fluctuations of the orbital energies and the magnetic field. The optimal operating points do not maximize the thermophase but balance a large quasiparticle response against sensitivity to parameter fluctuations. Under experimentally motivated noise assumptions, we obtain projected noise-equivalent temperatures of order $10\,\mu\mathrm{K}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and determine the range over which a linear calibration remains accurate. Gate-tunable quantum-dot junctions thus offer a phase-based route to sensing temperature differences in superconducting circuits at sub-kelvin temperatures.

title: Perfect Spin-to-Charge Signal Conversion via Inverse Spin Hall Effect in a Superconductor
summary: Spin-to-charge conversion is central to spintronics, but conventional spin Hall mechanisms are intrinsically limited by the small spin Hall angle. Here we show that superconductivity can overcome this limitation and enable near-unity spin-to-charge signal conversion. We consider a nonlocal spin-valve geometry in which a spin accumulation is injected into a superconductor and converted into a transverse charge signal through the inverse spin Hall effect. In the superconducting state, the strongly suppressed quasiparticle conductance below the gap allows the resulting charge imbalance to generate a voltage comparable to the injected spin bias, despite a small spin Hall angle. We derive the full nonequilibrium response including finite spectral broadening and finite temperature, and propose temperature and spin-bias-dependent measurements of the detector voltage to test our predictions.

title: Self-consistent Floquet theory of steady-state ordering in driven open systems
summary: Periodically driven open systems have quasienergy bands whose steady-state occupations are set by the drive and reservoir. We formulate a self-consistent Floquet spectral theory of electronic ordering in the weak-reservoir-coupling limit, expressing the nonlinear mean-field equation and the particle-hole response in terms of quasienergies, steady-state occupations, and harmonic matrix elements that account for micromotion. We illustrate the theory in the square-lattice Hubbard model and show how the drive produces `dynamical nesting' conditions and how Floquet resonances produce \textit{hysteretic} responses due to multiple self-consistent solutions. Interestingly, we find that the hysteresis branches exhibit distinct Floquet topologies. Away from half-filling, we find that the combination of drive-induced detuning of the van Hove saddle points and the micromotion leads to the onset of switching between competing incommensurate orders.

title: A Fractional Chern Semimetal: Exact Wavefunction and Conformal Criticality
summary: Unlike fractional quantum Hall states in uniform Landau levels, fractional Chern insulators can host dispersive anyon bands, raising the question of what happens when the anyon gap closes. We construct an exact finite-bond-dimension tensor-network state for a fractional Chern semimetal by Gutzwiller projecting a critical parton state. This state exhibits divergent correlation lengths in charged sectors but a fractionally quantized many-body Chern number of $1/3$. Although it has one electron per unit cell, its modular $S$ and $T$ matrices and entanglement spectrum match those of the $\nu=1/3$ Laughlin state. We identify a $(1+1)$--dimensional $U(3)_1\times SU(3)_1$ conformal field theory (CFT) governing the wavefunction norm in the infrared, an unexpected result for a state with $U(1)_3$ topology. The $SU(3)_1$ sector is a nonlinear sigma model whose Wess--Zumino level and kinetic stiffness are determined by the parton Chern number and Fubini--Study metric, respectively. Under renormalization, it flows to the conformal fixed point, with an initial distance to this fixed point controlled by the idealness of parton quantum geometry. Favorable geometry enables precise agreement with CFT predictions even on narrow cylinders.

title: Quantum-geometry-tuned Mott transition and emergent heavy fermions in a topological flat band
summary: A flat band with a nonzero Chern number has no localized Wannier orbitals, which raises the question of whether Mott physics is still possible. We place a Hubbard interaction $U$ on coherent orbitals, which are localized but overcomplete, and develop a single-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for this model. Within the flat band alone, DMFT reproduces the experimentally observed cascade and inverse-compressibility sawtooth without invoking Dirac revival or remote-band electrons. At nonzero integer filling we find an insulator-to-metal transition tuned by $s^2$, the fraction of the Brillouin zone that carries the Berry curvature. For $N_f=8$ flavors the Mott transition at $\nu=-2$ occurs at $s^2_c\approx0.025$, where the top of the lower Hubbard band reaches the Fermi level and the local moments are Kondo screened, forming a heavy Fermi liquid (HFL). The HFL extends to the hole-doped side, $\nu=-2-x$, but above the small Kondo temperature $T_K$ the state is an incoherent bad metal without a Fermi surface. At low temperature, an anti-Hund's coupling $J_A\sim0.1U$ replaces the HFL with a pseudogap metal that has a small Fermi surface and is dominated by spin-polaron excitations at small $x$. We propose this pseudogap metal as the parent state of superconductivity in TBG. The framework may also be applied to other topological bands, such as those of twisted WSe$_2$.

title: Strain-transfer at the Cu nanoparticle-Si(111) interface: static atomistic modelling and simulated Bragg CDI
summary: Substrate strain offers a route to control deformation in supported metallic nanoparticles, provided that interfacial coupling transmits the imposed loading into the particle. We assess this feasibility using five static Cu/Si(111) configurations spanning 0-2% biaxial tensile substrate strain. A 211,288-atom Cu particle is supported by a nominally 50 x 50 x 20 nm Si slab with its bottom 1 nm fixed, using the Jelinek modified embeddedatom potential. Relative to the relaxed supported 0% state, Cu-only local fits reveal heterogeneous, anisotropic deformation: particle-wide mean hydrostatic strain is negative at every nonzero loading, from -3.12 x 10-6 to -8.84 x 10-6, while the upper-particle mean varies nonmonotonically. Simulated Bragg CDI of Cu(111), obtained by inversion of known complex atomic scattering amplitudes, maps loading-dependent projected displacement and strain. The combined atomistic and Bragg CDI representations provide strong preliminary support for the feasibility of substrate-mediated strain transfer in this idealized system and identify spatial signatures for experimental investigation. Experiments remain indispensable to confirm transfer in real Cu/Si(111) nanoparticles and determine its magnitude.

title: Structural, optoelectronic, mechanical, thermodynamic and thermoelectric properties of kesterite Cu2ZnSnS4: A first-principles study
summary: The structural, optoelectronic, mechanical, thermodynamic, and thermoelectric properties of kesterite Cu2ZnSnS4 were investigated using density functional theory. The mBJ and HSE06 approaches yield band gaps of 0.88 and 1.55 eV, respectively. Optical calculations reveal high absorption, with the onset in the 0.8-1.0 eV range. Hydrostatic compression from 0 to 30 kbar decreases the lattice parameters and increases the band gap. The elastic constants satisfy the Born stability criterion, and B/G $>$ 1.75 indicates plastic behavior. Phonon calculations confirm dynamic stability. In the temperature range from 0 to 1000 K, the Helmholtz free energy decreases, the vibrational entropy increases, and the heat capacity approaches a plateau above 500 K. The thermoelectric properties were investigated in the temperature range from 100 to 1000 K. The Seebeck coefficient remains positive, peaking at approximately 310 $\mu$V/K at 250 K and decreasing to 239 $\mu$V/K at 1000 K. These results encourage the investigation of Cu2ZnSnS4 as a good candidate for thermoelectric power conversion.

title: Physically Informed Data-Driven Modeling of Low-Pressure Carburizing (LPC): A Self-Calibrating Boundary Condition for Carbon Flux
summary: This paper formulates an extended framework for a hybrid physically informed data-driven model of low-pressure carburizing (LPC), in which diffusive carbon transport in austenite is described by a physical equation, whereas the effective carbon flux across the gas-metal interface is treated as an unknown boundary forcing to be identified from experimental and process data. The basis for this formulation is that, in LPC, the most uncertain part of the model is not bulk diffusion but the transient surface kinetics of carbon uptake by the metal. In contrast to direct empirical relationships of the 'process regime-result' type, the proposed scheme uses machine learning as a closure operator for the boundary condition in the diffusion problem. This operator is calibrated using carbon concentration profiles, integral mass gain, surface concentration, effective case depth, and additional process measurements. Theoretically, the model is positioned as an operator-learning problem in a system constrained by a partial differential equation, physical flux constraints, inverse-problem regularization, and uncertainty quantification. The relationships between the proposed approach and physics-informed neural networks, operator learning, dynamic-system identification, boundary-operator learning, and boundary-control problems are considered. The mathematical formulation, calibration functional, identifiability conditions, preliminary tuning algorithm, and online adaptation scheme are formulated. The proposed approach is considered as a computational basis for developing interpretable digital support for LPC processes.

title: Defect Engineering of the Water-Carbon Interface: Insights from First-Principles Calculations
summary: Interactions at solid-liquid interfaces are fundamental to hydrovoltaic and catalytic technologies. While carbon nanomaterials have been extensively studied, the role of abundant defects in amorphous carbon remains poorly understood. Here, using first-principles calculations, we systematically investigate how various defects (topological, point, line, edge, and doping defects) modulate water-carbon interactions. We find that armchair-edge defects with dangling bonds reduce the energy barrier for water dissociation by up to 30 times compared with pristine carbon, while di-vacancies exhibit a near-zero Gibbs free energy for hydrogen evolution, enabling potential hydrogen evolution reaction activity on a purely carbon-based interface. Moreover, mono-vacancy defects, characterized by reduced electronic localization, enhance charge transfer to evaporating water molecules by up to 12.4 times, a key factor in evaporation-induced electricity generation. Crucially, we demonstrate that coupling distinct defects produces synergistic effects that outperform individual defects, revealing a promising strategy for designing multifunctional interfaces. These insights establish a defect-engineering framework for the rational design of high-efficiency hydrovoltaic and catalytic devices.

title: Metal to Semiconductor Transition in Niobium Sulfoselenide Alloy Films by Compositional Control
summary: Transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have garnered significant interest due to their tunable bandgaps, optical anisotropy, and mechanical flexibility. This study explores the relationship between stoichiometry, structural phase, and electronic transport in niobium sulfoselenide (NbSxSe2-x) thin films. In this study, low-dimensional TMD films were grown with molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) to investigate the effects of varying chalcogen (sulfur and selenium) content in NbSxSe2-x alloys. We focus on tuning electrical resistivity along with the transition from metallic-to-semiconducting behavior through compositional control. These MBE grown films were characterized using in-vacuo x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze the chemical composition. Electrical resistivity of the films and their temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) were extracted to determine their metallic and semiconducting behavior. Our results show that increasing sulfur content induces a transition from metallic to semiconducting behavior in NbSe2, accompanied by a rise in resistivity. This work highlights the potential for compositional tuning of TMDs for applications in tunable nanoelectronics.

title: First-Principles Investigation of the {ScSe2} TMDs Monolayer: Structural Stability, Electronic and Optical Properties
summary: We present an ab initio investigation of the {ScSe2} monolayer using density functional theory (DFT), as employed in the CP2K code, to assess its structural stability and electronic properties. The electronic behavior of both phases is governed by the local coordination environment of scandium and the associated lifting of degeneracy of its $3d$ orbitals. The valence bands (VBs) are dominated by {Se}$-4p$ states in both phases, while the states near the Fermi level distinguish the metallic 1T phase from the semiconducting 2H phase. Optical response calculations reveal markedly different spectral signatures for the two polymorphs. Two findings emerge from this study: a polymorphism-driven metal-to-semiconductor transition without any change in chemical composition and distinct optical responses relevant to phase-selective optoelectronic devices.

title: A Covalent Bonding Network Using p-Block Elements to Stabilize Lithium-Rich Cathode Materials
summary: Li-rich battery cathodes (LixMyOz, where x > y) have sparked significant attention for their high energy densities, but their practical application is currently limited by structural instabilities associated with high-valent redox. Recent work has demonstrated reversible high-potential (de)lithiation with low voltage hysteresis in Li4FeSbO6 (LFSO), but the stabilization mechanism for this unique charging behavior is not fully understood, limiting our ability to apply insights from LFSO to more earth-abundant cathodes. In this paper, we present a covalent Sb-O bonding network in LFSO which is facilitated by the p-block orbital character of Sb. Using ab initio computational modeling, we identify this bonding state and indicate its contributions to crystal stability; we also identify a signature for this bonding network using theoretical and experimental element-specific X-ray spectroscopy. Substituting Sb with other p-block elements preserves this stabilizing bond, pointing to a family of new cathode chemistries beyond LFSO. This work establishes a design principle for development of sustainable energy-dense batteries: p-block elements like Sb possess specific orbital-mediated oxygen bonding which contributes to stability of high-valent layered oxide cathodes.

title: Persistent Neutron Irradiation Effects and Partial Recovery in Thin-Film CdS/CdTe Solar Cells
summary: Thin-film CdTe solar cells are promising candidates for lightweight space power, but device-level studies of their response to neutron irradiation remain scarce. Here, we report the device performance of CdS/CdTe solar cells irradiated for 10 to 150 min in the thermal irradiator of a TRIGA reactor (90 kW), corresponding to nominal total neutron fluences of 3.3 x 10^14 to 5.0 x 10^15 n cm-2. The cells were characterized after 18 months of post-irradiation storage, once the residual activity has decayed to background levels. Co-irradiated FTO-coated glass reference substrates exhibit a wavelength-dependent transmission loss, with the transmittance at 500 nm decreasing from 80 % to 50 % after 60 min of irradiation. The irradiated cells retain rectifying behavior, but the reverse-bias dark current, photocurrent, and efficiency generally decrease with exposure time. Post-irradiation annealing at 70 {\deg}C under one-sun illumination initially improves Jsc and Voc, with the highest efficiency after 4 h. Prolonged annealing, however, causes substantial FF degradation despite continued photocurrent recovery. These trends suggest that irradiation-induced changes in the glass substrate, CdTe absorber, and contacts respond differently to annealing. Understanding underlying defect chemistry and correlating it with device behavior are necessary steps toward radiation-tolerant CdTe photovoltaics for space applications.

title: Interstitial Magnetoelectricity in Altermagnetic Electrides
summary: Electrides and altermagnets are two distinct yet intriguing classes of quantum materials, characterized by interstitial anionic electrons and nonrelativistic spin splitting, respectively. The recent prediction of Stoner-instability-driven altermagnetic electride provides a natural bridge between these two fields. Here, we investigate the magnetoelectric response and its related spin-polarized transport in the altermagnetic electride Zr$_2$N monolayer. Using the tight-binding Hubbard model and first-principles calculations, we find that the electric field can break the magnetic compensation between the two interstitial anionic electrons, inducing a finite net magnetization and giving rise to an interstitial electron mediated magnetoelectric response. The magnetoelectric response is further demonstrated through the electrical control of spin conductivity. Our results reveal a magnetoelectric effect in altermagnetic electrides, paving a way towards electride-based spintronic devices.

title: Ultrahigh Thermal Conductivity and Mirror-Parity Constraints in a Corrugated Two-Dimensional Oxide
summary: Contrary to the expectation of poor heat transport in oxides, first-principles calculations predict an ultrahigh lattice thermal conductivity of 756 $\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ at 300 K in corrugated two-dimensional B$_2$O$_2$. Acoustic phonons dominate heat transport, with the flexural acoustic (ZA) branch contributing 40.62$\%$. Triplet resolved analysis including acoustic and optical partners finds that mirror forbidden three phonon scattering is negligible within numerical precision for sampled ZA modes. These results highlight horizontal mirror symmetry as a constraint on phonon scattering in corrugated oxides.

title: Tritium speciation and transport in molten FLiBe: parameters, uncertainties and validation priorities
summary: Molten lithium fluoride-beryllium fluoride (FLiBe) is a candidate liquid breeder material for fusion applications, but predictive modelling of tritium retention, transport and extraction depends on chemical and interfacial assumptions that remain only partly resolved. Tritium produced in lithium-bearing fluoride salts may occur in oxidised or fluoride-associated states and can exchange into molecular hydrogen-isotope species such as HT. The relative populations and apparent transport behaviour depend on salt composition and condition, redox state, and interactions at gas-liquid and salt-wall boundaries. This review assesses the evidence for tritium speciation and transport in molten FLiBe, with emphasis on the solubility, effective diffusivity, permeability, exchange and boundary-transfer parameters required by continuum models. The available evidence motivates a two-pool continuum description with separate oxidised or fluoride-associated and molecular-hydrogen pools, without assigning a unique microscopic species. This description applies where states omitted from these pools do not materially affect tritium inventory or transport in the salt. We distinguish directly measured quantities from fitted or inferred effective parameters, recommend how source-specific transport data should be reported and compared, and identify the measurements required to constrain the remaining uncertainties in speciation, exchange, bulk transport and boundary transfer.

title: Synthesis Method-dependent Resist-like Behavior of Liquid Crystalline Graphene Oxide Films Under Electron Beam Irradiation
summary: Here, the electron-beam-induced structural evolution and patterning behavior of chitosan-functionalized GO films, specifically those using chemically vs electrochemically exfoliated GO, are investigated. Experimental results (supported by DFT calculations) revealed that electron irradiation drives controllable microstructure formation in GO by selectively triggering ablation and densification pathways, which are dictated by the GOs synthesis route and initial oxidation state. Furthermore, a comprehensive characterization study was conducted to compare the optostructural properties of the present system prior and subsequent to electron-beam irradiation. Moreover, a systematic study of the films mechanical properties across both micro- and macroscopic scales was also performed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms responsible for the observed phenomena. The results demonstrate that the integration of mask-free electron-beam patterning, multiscale characterization, and DFT modeling establishes a previously unexplored synthesis-structure-irradiation relationship in GO films, providing fundamental insights into irradiation-induced microstructure evolution and opening new avenues for the design of GO-based micro- and nanostructured materials.

title: DeepDOSReasoner: Physics-Grounded Reasoning for Density-of-States Prediction and Materials Discovery
summary: Predicting a material's behavior from its atomic structure is a longstanding goal of the physical sciences. The electronic and phonon densities of states (eDOS and phDOS) govern key electronic, optical, vibrational, and thermodynamic properties, yet their calculation using density functional theory (DFT) is costly: about 60% of Materials Project entries lack eDOS and over 80% lack phDOS. Existing crystal-to-spectrum models rely on pooled structural representations and pointwise regression, which blur spectral features and violate total-state conservation. Here we introduce DeepDOSReasoner, a physics-grounded framework that decodes spectra through atom-to-energy source attention and refines the normalized DOS through learned continuity-equation transport, enforcing nonnegativity and total-state conservation by construction. DeepDOSReasoner achieves the highest prediction accuracy across all evaluated metrics for both eDOS and phDOS, recovers element-resolved contributions without supervision, and most reliably identifies rare valence-band (VB) gaps. In a prospective screen of 8,106 uncharted materials validated by new DFT calculations, its predictions remain the most accurate among the methods evaluated, with 25 of its top 50 candidates confirmed as VB-gap materials. Three case studies spanning substituted compounds, photovoltaic chalcogenides, and a high-entropy alloy demonstrate transfer across materials classes. Ablations confirm that both stages are necessary, while the model retains comparable accuracy when trained on only 25% of the data. Predicting spectra in milliseconds enables exhaustive screening; we release predictions filling the missing eDOS for 91,405 and phDOS for 127,768 Materials Project entries. DeepDOSReasoner provides a blueprint for integrating machine learning with physical reasoning toward high-throughput spectral screening and autonomous materials discovery.

title: CLFF: Automated Framework for Concurrent Learning Force Fields and Material Property Calculations
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer an efficient paradigm for large-scale atomistic simulations with near first-principles accuracy. However, developing and deploying these potentials often involves intricate procedures that require substantial manual effort and domain expertise. In this work, we present CLFF, an open-source Python framework designed to automate concurrent learning workflows for MLIPs. CLFF integrates model training, MLIP-driven sampling, uncertainty-based candidate selection, quantum-mechanical labeling, and dataset augmentation into a unified workflow. The framework currently supports several modern graph-based MLIP architectures and is compatible with widely used computational chemistry and materials science tools. A distinguishing feature of CLFF is its ability to asynchronously distribute computational tasks across multiple heterogeneous remote computing resources, enabling users to aggregate fragmented hardware infrastructure within a single controllable workflow. In addition to concurrent learning, CLFF provides automated workflows for initial data generation and material property calculations, including phonon dispersion and potential energy surface scans. By minimizing manual intervention and enhancing reproducibility, CLFF offers a flexible platform for developing and deploying MLIPs in computational materials research.

title: AgenticMM: A Material-Centered Multi-Agent Architecture for Scalable First-Principles Materials Modeling
summary: Multi-agent frameworks are attracting increasing attention as a means of autonomously driving complex, long-running workflows in first-principles materials modeling. However, such frameworks commonly organize AI agents by computational task or scientific role. When scaled across many materials, this organization can require repeated transfers of material-specific context and complicate persistent execution and resource coordination. Here, we introduce AgenticMM, a material-centered multi-agent architecture in which each material has a persistent agent that owns its complete workflow and retains its scientific context, while a persistent coordinator allocates shared resources, mediates communication, and tracks campaign progress. AgenticMM is designed to incorporate reusable, prompt-based skills as modular definitions of these workflows. Using DefectSkills prompts, we demonstrate the feasibility of AgenticMM through a multistage point-defect campaign in which material-specific agents concurrently perform host electronic-structure, phase-stability, and intrinsic-defect calculations for five chemically diverse semiconductors.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Accurate Quasiparticle Energy Levels in Large Supercells of Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
summary:
The GW method is the one of the main workhorses of the materials science community to accurately calculate the electronic bandgap of materials, as it overcomes the gap underestimation problem from Density Functional Theory (DFT). Despite its accuracy, its computational cost becomes prohibitive when calculations have more than 10-100 atoms, which makes more difficult its use for defects, surfaces and moir\'e systems that demand large supercells. To overcome this problem, we developed a Graph Neural Network trained with smaller GW calculations which can make accurate predictions on large supercells at a small fraction of the computational cost.
  Our model uses as features the projection of DFT wavefunctions into localized atomic orbitals, while graph nodes represent the atomic positions and edges represent atom to atom distances, which captures the system geometry. We explore how to do "small AI", providing a workflow of how to create a personal and convenient dataset of GW calculations to train the model that can be applied to different materials so that the final user does not need to rely on massive datasets. We define what must be included in the training dataset to capture the physics of our objective simulation, and perform a Bayesian optimization of hyperparameters. In the case of monolayer MoS$_2$ with a sulfur vacancy our GNN models achieve high accuracy (MAE ranging 10 to 50 meV) with a simplified workflow applicable to other materials, accelerating accurate large electronic structure calculations.

title: Collineations of particles as a tool to study nucleation and crystallization processes in liquids
summary: We suggest several methods that can be used for identification of crystal nuclei in the studies of the nucleation and crystallization processes in multicomponent systems and in situations when the forming crystalline phase is different from the FCC, HCP or BCC lattices. We suggest several methods that can be used for identification of crystal nuclei in the studies of the nucleation and crystallization processes in multicomponent systems and in situations when the forming crystalline phase is different from the FCC, HCP or BCC lattices. The approaches are based on consideration of collineations of particles. They allow finding nuclei and separating them from each other. We demonstrate the methods by considering two systems. For a single-component system, we perform a comparison between the results derived from the collineations and those obtained using the coarse-grained bond-orientational order parameters. Further, we illustrate the methods by considering the crystallization process in a Wahnstr\"{o}m binary $BA_2$ system forming a rather complex crystal structure.

title: Fully solid-state all-2D micro-supercapacitors for on-chip energy storage
summary: Integrating energy storage directly into microelectronic platforms remains a major challenge. Although solid-state micro-supercapacitors (MSCs) have been previously demonstrated, most still rely on liquid or solvent-containing gel electrolytes, which require additional encapsulation and complicate device integration. Here, we demonstrate wafer-scale fabrication of all-2D, fully solid-state MSCs by combining conductive Ti3C2Tz MXene electrodes with a natural vermiculite (VMT) clay solid electrolyte. Both materials are solution-processable and can be independently patterned using microelectronics compatible fabrication techniques, allowing for their integration across 4-inch Si/SiO2 wafers. The resulting devices showcase an active stack of only 28 nm thick, with an areal capacitance of 205 uF/cm2 and volumetric energy density of ~15.5 mWh/cm3. Notably, this work introduces a patterned 2D clay as a solid electrolyte in an on-chip electrochemical energy-storage device, extending the role of layered materials beyond electrodes to ion-conducting components. To investigate device behavior and degradation, we employ non-destructive imaging ellipsometry to map individual layer thicknesses and extract the spatial distribution of MXene conductivity across the chip. This approach reveals localized changes in electrode properties following prolonged electrochemical cycling, providing insight into degradation processes that are difficult to capture using conventional spatially averaged measurements. Together, these results establish a route towards fully solid-state, all-2D energy-storage devices and highlight the potential of solution-processable layered materials for integration into microelectronic systems.

title: Engineering strategies for high-performance self-powered zinc oxide (ZnO) ultraviolet photodetectors: a design-oriented review
summary: Self-powered ultraviolet (UV) photodetectors generate a signal at zero applied bias, removing standby power and suppressing dark current, suiting battery-free Internet-of-Things sensing. Zinc oxide (ZnO) is the archetypal absorber for this task: UV-selective, earth-abundant, non-toxic, and processable at low temperature from solution. Operating it without bias, however, requires a built-in asymmetry that pristine ZnO rarely provides. Because the literature is organized by material or mechanism, the design logic remains obscured. Here we organize the field by engineering strategy, identifying five families of levers (junction and built-in-field engineering, doping and defect control, polarization coupling, interface/surface and photoelectrochemical engineering, and architecture and light management) and mapping each onto the metrics it serves and the trade-offs it imposes. A unifying lens is the zero-bias doping paradox: raising carrier density narrows the depletion region that zero-bias collection needs, so the self-powered optimum differs from the biased one. We flag the detectivity, speed, and active-area pitfalls that make zero-bias performance easy to overstate, and condense the synthesis into a decision tree linking target metric to strategy and growth route. The remaining bottlenecks (persistent photoconductivity, p-type ZnO, and reporting consistency) are problems of defect control and rigorous measurement, not of new materials.

title: Ballistic propagation-mediated super-resolution light-element imaging: in-situ tracking dynamic hydrogen migration
summary: Transmission electrons - with few-picometer wavelengths - can theoretically resolve all atoms in solids. However, constrained by factors such as lens aberrations, Z-contrast dependence and poor temporal resolution, the scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) fails to tackle the long-standing challenge of hydrogen dynamics on atomic scale.
